title: Episode 306: Henry V: Agincourt, the St. Crispin's Day Brotherhood, and the Crown of France
description:
The electrifying life of King Henry V, the greatest warrior monarch in English history. Transforming from a wild, reckless prince into a focused, austere, and brilliant military genius, Henry ascended the throne in 1413 with one single-minded purpose: to conquer the kingdom of France. In 1415, after a brutal siege at Harfleur and marching an exhausted, dysentery-stricken army through the mud of northern France, Henry found his path blocked by a massive French chivalric army at Agincourt. Outnumbered four to one, Henry deployed his legendary yeomen longbowmen and wooden stakes on St. Crispin's Day to achieve one of the most stunning underdog victories in world military annals. Conquering Normandy and securing the French crown by treaty, discover the legend of Henry the Fifth.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series chronicles the sovereign whose battlefield genius forged England's greatest military legend, uniting prince and yeoman in an immortal band of brothers: King Henry V. Here is George with the magnificent story of Agincourt, the longbow, and the conqueror of France.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: PRINCE HAL: THE MAKING OF A WARRIOR: 1386 TO 1413
Born in September 1386 in the gatehouse tower of Monmouth Castle on the Welsh border, Henry of Monmouth was twelve years old when his father usurped the throne. When his father seized power, young Henry was placed in the household of King Richard II in Ireland, who treated the boy with genuine kindness, knighting him on the battlefield. When Bolingbroke became Henry IV, Hal was invested as Prince of Wales and immediately thrust into brutal mountain warfare against Owain Glyndŵr. Between the ages of fourteen and twenty-two, Hal spent nearly a decade in the saddle, learning logistics, artillery siegecraft, and tactical leadership in the rugged Welsh hills. At the Battle of Shrewsbury in 1403, when a rebel bodkin arrow penetrated six inches into his skull beneath his right eye, court surgeon John Bradmore performed an astonishing medical miracle, designing a specialized threaded metal extractor to screw into the hollow socket of the arrowhead and extract it without killing the prince. Though Shakespeare later popularized the myth of Prince Hal as a dissolute tavern brawler cavorting with Sir John Falstaff at the Boar's Head, the historical Henry was deeply serious, pious, austere, and possessed of an iron administrative discipline. When his father died in March 1413, twenty-six-year-old Henry V immediately cast aside worldly frivolity, dedicating his life to a divine calling: uniting England and claiming the crown of France. Young Henry's years on the Welsh border transformed him into an unmatched military technician: he became an expert in the use of gunpowder artillery, cannon trajectories, and logistics trains. He lived alongside his common foot soldiers in open bivouacs, eating the same coarse salt beef and bread, earning a fierce, unbreakable devotion from the Welsh and English archers who would follow him to the gates of Paris.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SOUTHAMPTON PLOT AND THE VOYAGE TO FRANCE: 1415
From his first moments on the throne, Henry V pursued a policy of national reconciliation at home and audacious aggression abroad. He reburied the murdered Richard II with solemn royal honors in Westminster Abbey and restored the heirs of his father's enemies to their lands. Turning his eyes toward France, which was torn apart by civil war between the Armagnacs and Burgundians while its king, Charles VI, suffered from recurring bouts of madness believing he was made of glass, Henry formally demanded the full restoration of the Angevin Empire and the hand of Princess Catherine of Valois. When French dauphin Louis supposedly sent Henry a mocking insult of tennis balls—insinuating he was better suited to playground games than war—Henry coldly replied that he would play a game in France that would knock the French crown into the hazard. On the eve of his departure from Southampton in July 1415, a treasonous conspiracy known as the Southampton Plot was uncovered to replace Henry with Edmund Mortimer. Henry acted with terrifying speed: the conspirators, including his own cousin the Earl of Cambridge, were tried, condemned, and beheaded outside Southampton's Bargate within days. On August 11, 1415, Henry set sail across the Channel with a fleet of fifteen hundred ships and twelve thousand men. The tennis balls incident, whether factual or courtly propaganda, captured the arrogant dismissal of the French nobility toward the young English king. Henry's chillingly swift execution of Cambridge, Scrope, and Grey outside Southampton showed his terrifying zero-tolerance policy for treason, securing his home front so completely that not a single rebellion occurred in England during his absence.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SIEGE OF HARFLEUR: BLOOD, MUD, AND DYSENTERY
Henry landed at the mouth of the River Seine and immediately laid siege to the heavily fortified port city of Harfleur, which he intended to turn into a second Calais. For five grueling weeks under a sweltering late-summer sun, Henry's army battered the massive stone ramparts with giant siege guns firing five-hundred-pound stone balls. But the swampy terrain around Harfleur proved deadly: an epidemic of bloody flux—severe dysentery—swept through the English camp. Over two thousand soldiers perished in their tents, and another two thousand had to be invalided back to England, including key noble commanders. When Harfleur finally surrendered on September 22, Henry had lost a third of his entire force, leaving him with barely six thousand men, of whom five thousand were longbowmen and barely one thousand were men-at-arms. His experienced war council urged an immediate return to England by sea. Henry refused. He insisted that honor demanded he march his small army two hundred and sixty miles across northern France to the English stronghold at Calais to demonstrate to God and the world that he was the rightful ruler of France. For over two weeks, his exhausted, half-starved, and shivering soldiers trudged through relentless autumn downpours, only to find the bridges across the River Somme destroyed and French cavalry shadowing every move. At Harfleur, Henry ordered his gunners to keep up a relentless twenty-four-hour bombardment, shattering the medieval stone towers. Yet when the city fell, he forbade his men from looting or harming women and churches, hanging any soldier caught stealing so much as a consecrated pyx, maintaining iron moral discipline even as his soldiers died in hundreds from dysentery.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE EVE OF ST. CRISPIN: OCTOBER 24, 1415
Finally discovering an unguarded ford across the Somme near Péronne, Henry crossed the river and pushed toward Calais. But on the afternoon of October 24, near the tiny hamlet of Maisoncelle, English scouts crested a ridge and halted in shock: blocking their path across the narrow valley between the dense woods of Agincourt and Tramecourt stood a colossal French army. The French chivalric host, commanded by Constable Charles d'Albret and the Duke of Orléans, numbered between twenty and thirty thousand men—outnumbering the ragged English army by more than four to one. That night, as torrential rain poured down upon the plowed fields, turning the clay soil into a quagmire of deep mud, the two camps presented a study in contrast. In the French camp, confident nobles feasted, drank wine, played dice for the ransoms of English lords, and bragged of the easy slaughter awaiting them at dawn. In the English camp, strict silence was commanded under pain of death. Shivering around sputtering campfires in the freezing mud, English archers confessed their sins to chaplains, greased their bowstrings, and sharpened six-foot ash stakes to points at both ends. Henry walked among his men in the dark, visiting sentries and speaking words of calm, iron faith. It was the eve of the Feast of Saints Crispin and Crispinian. The ground between Agincourt and Tramecourt had been freshly plowed for winter wheat, and the twenty-four hours of torrential rain turned the loam into a viscous soup that sucked the iron-shod boots off men's feet. The English archers, stripped to their linen undergarments and bare feet to move swiftly through the mud, stood shivering in the dark, knowing that the French had vowed to cut off the three shooting fingers of every captured archer.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE BATTLE OF AGINCOURT: OCTOBER 25, 1415
At dawn on October 25, Henry drew up his six thousand men in a narrow clearing barely eight hundred yards wide between the two dense forests, effectively neutralizing the French advantage in numbers. He placed dismounted men-at-arms in the center and arrayed wings of Welsh and English archers on the flanks, protected by a palisade of sharp wooden stakes driven into the mud angled toward the enemy. Wearing a glittering gold crown encircling his bascinet helmet adorned with the Black Prince's ruby, Henry addressed his troops: 'We few, we happy few, we band of brothers!' When the French refused to advance across the mud, Henry took an audacious risk: he ordered his archers to pull up their stakes, advance within longbow range, re-plant their stakes, and open fire. The first devastating volley provoked an impetuous French cavalry charge. Warhorses slipped, floundered, and collapsed in the knee-deep clay as clouds of bodkin arrows pierced horse armor and riders. When the massed French dismounted men-at-arms charged on foot, weighed down by sixty pounds of plate armor, the narrow funnel forced them into a suffocating crush where they could barely swing their swords. English archers dropped their bows, drew lead-weighted mallets, axes, and daggers, and swarmed into the melee. Within three hours, the French army was destroyed: over six thousand Frenchmen lay dead, including the Constable, three dukes, and ninety lords, while English losses were fewer than two hundred. When a small French raiding party struck the English baggage train during the battle, Henry made the ruthless and controversial decision to order the execution of the French prisoners, fearing they would take up arms from the corpses and strike his men from behind. His men-at-arms initially refused out of chivalric honor, prompting Henry to dispatch two hundred archers to carry out the grim order until the crisis passed.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE TREATY OF TROYES: CROWN OF FRANCE: 1420
Agincourt shattered the military prestige of France and established Henry V as the supreme sovereign of Europe. Returning to London in triumph, where ecstatic crowds showered him with golden leaves, Henry did not rest on his laurels. In 1417, he launched a systematic, brilliantly organized amphibious campaign to conquer the entire Duchy of Normandy, capturing Caen, Cherbourg, and finally Rouen after a grueling six-month siege in which twelve thousand starving citizens expelled from the city were left to die in the freezing castle ditches. With Normandy secured and the French nobility fatally divided following the assassination of the Duke of Burgundy by the Dauphin's men, the new Burgundian duke allied with Henry. In May 1420, Henry dictated the Treaty of Troyes to the French court. Under its historic terms, French King Charles VI disinherited his own son, the Dauphin, and declared Henry V his legitimate heir and Regent of France. To seal the dynastic union, Henry married Princess Catherine of Valois in June 1420 at Troyes Cathedral. Entering Paris in triumph at Christmas, Henry was hailed as the sovereign of a dual Anglo-French monarchy. In December 1421, Catherine gave birth at Windsor to a son, Prince Henry, uniting the bloodlines of England and France. The siege of Rouen demonstrated the terrifying, unyielding iron of Henry's will: when the starving French city expelled twelve thousand women, children, and elderly citizens to conserve food, Henry refused to let them through English siege lines. Trapped in the frozen ditches in midwinter, thousands perished in agony between the walls and trenches, while Henry sent priests to baptize newborn babies before they froze to death.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE FATAL DYSENTERY AT VINCENNES AND THE UNFULFILLED VISION: 1422
At thirty-five years of age, Henry V stood on the absolute summit of human ambition. He had achieved what no Plantagenet king had ever accomplished: legal and military mastery over the realm of France. He envisioned leading a grand, united European crusade to recapture Jerusalem and liberate the Holy Land. But the ceaseless physical toll of winter sieges and battlefield campaigns had worn down his iron constitution. In the spring of 1422, while conducting the grueling seven-month siege of Meaux on the River Marne, Henry contracted a severe, agonizing case of dysentery—the very disease that had ravaged his army at Harfleur. Too weak to sit on his warhorse, he was carried in a horse litter toward Melun, but his fever worsened. Taken to the royal Château de Vincennes outside Paris, Henry lay dying in his bedchamber surrounded by his weeping commanders. He reaffirmed his loyalty to the Holy Church, appointed his brother the Duke of Bedford regent of France and the Duke of Gloucester protector of England, and whispered with his dying breath that if God had spared him, he would have rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. On August 31, 1422, just seven weeks before the death of King Charles VI would have officially crowned him King of France, Henry V died at the age of thirty-five. His body was brought back to England and buried in Westminster Abbey, leaving the dual crown to a helpless nine-month-old infant. When Henry lay dying at Vincennes, his doctors admitted there was no hope, informing him he had barely two hours to live. He called his confessors to chant the Seven Penitential Psalms; when the priest reached the verse 'Build thou the walls of Jerusalem,' the dying warrior whispered that it had been the sincere intention of his heart to liberate the Holy Sepulchre before closing his eyes forever.

[Rebecca - Host]
